message:
I'm redoing our downstairs bathroom floor myself (first time, slightly terrified) and I've got a pile of questions.

The tile shop guy talked really fast so I didn't catch half of it. Could you explain what "lippage" means in tiling, in simple terms? And what's a sensible grout colour for a pale grey porcelain tile if I don't want it looking dirty after a month? My partner also wants to know whether we should do the floor before or after the new toilet goes in, just a quick answer with a reason.

The floor is 2.4 m by 1.8 m. The tiles I like are 30 cm × 60 cm and come in boxes of 8. Everyone online says to add 10% for cuts and breakages. How many boxes do I actually need to buy?

I also need a short, polite message to the neighbours saying there'll be some noise from cutting tiles on Saturday morning, since they've already put up with a skip on the drive for a fortnight. Finally, any three tips for a beginner laying their first floor would be very welcome. I've watched a lot of videos, but they all make it look far easier than it probably is.

Thank you, honestly.
response:
Happy to help, and being slightly terrified on your first floor is normal. Here are your answers in order.

## What "lippage" means

Lippage is when one tile's edge sits higher than the tile next to it, leaving a little ledge where they meet. You can feel it with your fingers or your sock, and on a floor it catches dirt and can be a trip hazard. Long rectangular tiles like 30 × 60 cm are more prone to it, because they often have a slight bow along their length. That's why fitters often lay them offset by a third rather than by half, and use tile levelling clips to hold the edges flush while the adhesive sets.

## Grout colour

Choose a **mid grey, a shade or two darker than the tile**. With pale grey porcelain that will look neat and won't show dirt. White or very pale grout on a floor will look grubby within weeks. Very dark grout makes a strong grid that shows up any uneven joints. A stain-resistant grout, or sealing a standard cement grout, will help it stay clean.

## Floor or toilet first?

**Floor first, then the toilet.** The toilet then sits on finished tile, with no awkward cuts around its base and no gaps if you ever replace it with a different shape. Before you start, check that the new floor height still suits the toilet's waste connection.

## How many boxes

- Floor area: 2.4 × 1.8 = **4.32 m²**
- One tile: 0.3 × 0.6 = 0.18 m², so the floor takes **24 tiles**
- Plus 10%: 26.4, rounded up to **27 tiles**
- At 8 per box: 27 ÷ 8 = 3.4, so **buy 4 boxes** (32 tiles)

Three boxes would give exactly 24 tiles with no spares at all, so 4 is the right number. The 8 spare tiles also cover the extra cuts if you lay them offset, plus a couple to keep for future repairs.

Check that all 4 boxes have the **same batch number**, because shades can vary between batches.

## Message to the neighbours

> Hi both, just a quick heads-up that I'll be cutting tiles on Saturday morning, so there'll be some noise from about 9 until lunchtime. I'll keep it to the morning and get it done as quickly as I can. Thank you for being so patient with the skip on the drive too; it'll be gone soon. Do shout if Saturday morning is particularly bad for you. Thanks!

Adjust the times to suit your plans.

## Three tips for a first floor

1. **Prepare the subfloor properly.** It needs to be solid, clean and flat. Check it with a long straight edge and fix dips or bumps before you start. A timber floor usually needs overboarding with plywood or tile backer board first. Most tiling problems start here, and the videos tend to skip this part.
2. **Lay the tiles out dry before you glue anything.** Plan from the doorway, since that's what everyone sees first, and shift the layout so you don't end up with thin slivers along a wall or at the door.
3. **Work in small sections and get full adhesive coverage.** Mix small batches of adhesive and lay a small area at a time. Spread a thin layer on the back of each large tile ("back-buttering") as well as on the floor. Every so often, lift a freshly laid tile to check the back is fully covered. Leave a small gap around the edges of the room for expansion, and keep off the floor for 24 hours.

Good luck. Take it slowly, and if one tile goes wrong it's easy to lift and re-lay while the adhesive is still wet.
